title: Emotional Behaviour
summary: What emotions are, their bodily signatures, how emotional understanding develops socially, the brain structures and chemicals behind emotion, and how mood shapes thinking.

lesson.title: Feelings in the body and between people
lesson.hook: When you are angry, your face feels hot; when you are afraid, your hands go cold. Could a thermometer tell which emotion you are feeling?

slides.heading: What emotions are
slides.body:
**Emotions** give colour, meaning and intensity to life. They are usually **reactions to stimuli**, with **physiological arousal** and **characteristic behaviour**.

Watson and Tellegen (1985) argued that the many human emotions can be seen as combinations of just **two basic dimensions**: **positive** and **negative** feeling. Fear, for example, is acutely unpleasant, arouses the **sympathetic** nervous system, and shows in behaviour.

steps.title: Feeling
steps.detail: The subjective experience: pleasant or unpleasant, mild or intense.

steps.title: Physiological arousal
steps.detail: Bodily changes driven largely by the autonomic nervous system.

steps.title: Behaviour and expression
steps.detail: Facial expressions, posture and actions such as fleeing or attacking.

slides.heading: Faces and bodies match
slides.body:
**Ekman and colleagues (1983)** and **Levenson and colleagues (1990)** asked people to pose facial expressions of six emotions: **fear, anger, sadness, happiness, surprise and disgust**. Meanwhile they measured how fast the **heart** beat, how much the **skin conducted electricity** (sweating), how **warm the hands** were, and how **tense the forearm muscles** became.

Each posed expression produced its **own physiological pattern**, suggesting emotions have distinct bodily signatures.

slides.question: In Ekman's studies, which emotion was marked by high skin temperature compared with fear and sadness?
slides.why: Anger showed warmer skin; fear and sadness showed cooler skin, though all three raised heart rate.

slides.heading: Emotion as communication
slides.body:
From infancy, emotions are a **social signal** between baby and caregiver. Caregivers read the baby's signals, keep in time with them, and adjust the surroundings to keep stimulation at the **right level**.

**Field (1994)** called this **attunement**. Without it, the infant's behaviour can become **disorganised and chaotic**.

steps.title: Global empathy
steps.detail: The infant catches distress from others by emotional contagion and feels distressed too.

steps.title: Egocentric empathy
steps.detail: The child knows another is upset but responds as if their own feelings are the same.

steps.title: Others' feelings differ
steps.detail: The child understands another person's feelings can differ from their own.

steps.title: True empathy
steps.detail: Genuine understanding of another's experience, which supports cooperation towards shared goals.

slides.heading: The crying classmate
slides.story: In a crèche, when one baby cries, others start crying too: global empathy. At three, Dayo sees a friend crying and offers him his own favourite toy, assuming what comforts him will comfort his friend. By seven, Dayo asks what is wrong and fetches the friend's mother, because he knows the friend needs something different.
slides.takeaway: Empathy grows from emotional contagion to truly understanding another person's feelings, enabling cooperation.

slides.question: A baby starts crying simply because another baby nearby is crying. This is Hoffman's stage of:
slides.why: Catching distress through contagion, without understanding it, is global empathy.

slides.heading: How your lecturer will ask this
slides.body: Expect 'explain the social aspects of emotional development' with attunement and Hoffman's four stages, and objectives on Ekman's heart-rate and temperature findings. Trap: grouping disgust with high heart rate. Disgust, happiness and surprise went with lower heart rate.
slides.sampleQuestion: Field (1994) used the term 'attunement' to describe: (a) children's empathy (b) caregivers regulating infants' arousal by reading their signals (c) the amygdala's role (d) mood-congruent memory
slides.howToAnswer: Answer (b). In an essay, add that without attunement, infant behaviour becomes disorganised, then describe Hoffman's stages.

points: Emotions combine feeling, arousal and behaviour.
Watson and Tellegen: two basic dimensions, positive and negative.
Ekman: each emotion has its own bodily pattern.
Hoffman: global, egocentric, differing feelings, true empathy.

questions.stem: Watson and Tellegen (1985) proposed that emotions combine two basic elements:
questions.explanation: They reduced emotions to positive and negative dimensions.

questions.stem: Which branch of the nervous system is aroused when we feel fear?
questions.explanation: Fear triggers sympathetic, fight-or-flight arousal.

questions.stem: The first stage in Hoffman's development of empathy is:
questions.explanation: Global empathy, catching others' distress, comes first.

questions.stem: In Ekman's studies, lower heart rate was associated with:
questions.explanation: Happiness, disgust and surprise showed lower heart rate.

questions.stem: Field (1994) warned that without attunement, an infant's behaviour may become:
questions.explanation: Lack of caregiver attunement leads to disorganised behaviour.

questions.stem: In Hoffman's final stage, children develop:
questions.explanation: True empathy allows cooperation towards joint goals.

questions.stem: A participant posing an angry face shows rising heart rate and warmer hands. This matches findings by:
questions.explanation: Ekman found anger linked with high heart rate and high skin temperature.

questions.stem: A mother notices her baby is overstimulated by noise, dims the lights and rocks him until he calms. This is:
questions.explanation: Reading the infant's signals and adjusting the environment is attunement.

questions.stem: A four-year-old knows his sister is sad but offers her his own toy car, assuming it will cheer her as it cheers him. He is at:
questions.explanation: He recognises distress but responds through his own perspective.

questions.stem: All of the following were physiological measures in Ekman's studies EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: They measured heart rate, skin conductance, hand temperature and muscle tension, not MRI.

questions.stem: Which emotions showed low skin temperature relative to anger?
questions.explanation: Fear and sadness had cooler skin than anger.

questions.stem: Why is the development of true empathy important socially?
options: It lets people cooperate with peers to achieve joint goals
questions.explanation: Understanding others' perspectives supports cooperation.

questions.stem: I. Each posed facial expression matched a specific physiological pattern. II. Fear and anger both raised heart rate. III. Disgust raised heart rate more than anger. Which are correct?
questions.explanation: I and II are correct. Disgust was associated with lower heart rate.

questions.stem: Ekman's finding that posing a facial expression produced matching body changes suggests that:
options: Facial expressions are unrelated to physiology
Faces and bodily arousal are linked in emotion
questions.explanation: Distinct physiological patterns with posed faces point to tight face-body links.

questions.stem: Which sequence correctly orders Hoffman's stages?
options: True empathy, egocentric, global, differing feelings
Differing feelings, global, egocentric, true empathy
Egocentric, global, true empathy, differing feelings
Global, egocentric, differing feelings, true empathy
questions.explanation: Empathy develops from contagion to egocentric, to recognising differences, to true empathy.

lesson.title: Where emotions live and what they do to thought
lesson.hook: You jump back from a stick on the path before you even realise it looked like a snake. Your brain reacted to danger before 'you' knew about it. How?

slides.heading: Three ways to study the emotional brain

steps.title: Lesion method
steps.detail: Study effects of brain damage, accidental in people or surgical in animal experiments.

steps.title: Stimulation
steps.detail: Chemically or electrically stimulate a brain area and observe the behaviour that follows.

steps.title: Brain imaging
steps.detail: Use scans to see which regions become active as emotions change.

slides.heading: Hypothalamus and septum
slides.body:
The **hypothalamus**, below the thalamus, monitors **internal states** such as water balance, temperature and hormones, and organises **appropriate behaviour**.

Working with the **septum**, the hypothalamus handles **emotional and motivational** signals and helps arrange fitting responses, such as fleeing danger or seeking food.

slides.heading: The amygdala: emotional computer
slides.body:
The **amygdala** is a limbic structure (your course notes link it closely with the hypothalamus; anatomically it sits in the temporal lobe). It is often called the brain's **central emotional computer**.

**LeDoux (1993, 1996)** showed it receives input from cortical areas for **visual and auditory recognition**, and also **directly from the thalamus**. That direct route is fast but rough, which is why you can jump at a snake-shaped stick before you see it clearly.

slides.heading: LeDoux's two routes to the amygdala

right.title: Via the cortex
points: Can confirm or cancel the alarm

slides.question: According to LeDoux, the amygdala receives sensory information:
options: Both directly from the thalamus and from recognition areas of the cortex
slides.why: The direct thalamic route is fast; the cortical route is slower but more detailed.

terms.meaning: Released into the synapse to pass signals between nerve cells
Carried in the blood to affect organs sensitive to them
Often peptides that adjust signalling, for example in the pain system; some resemble opiates

slides.heading: Emotion shapes thinking
slides.body:
Emotions affect basic **cognitive processes**: perception, attention and memory. **Anxious** people are especially **vigilant for threat**, often involuntarily noticing danger cues others miss.

**Sad or depressed** people tend to **remember negative material**, especially past losses linked to how they feel now.

slides.heading: Mood-congruent memory
slides.body:
**Clark and Teasdale (1982)** studied people whose depression varied through the day. At their **most depressed** times, they recalled **more unhappy memories**; at their **least depressed** times, **more happy memories**.

This is **mood-congruent memory**: we more easily recall memories that **match our current mood**, which can keep a low mood going.

slides.question: Clark and Teasdale (1982) found that at their most depressed times of day, participants recalled:
slides.why: Recall matched current mood: more unhappy memories when most depressed, more happy ones when least depressed.

slides.heading: Two students, one exam
slides.story: Before a test, anxious Ngozi scans the hall and notices every frowning face and the invigilator's stern tone. Her calm friend Seun barely notices either. After failing an earlier test, Seun's low mood made him remember every past failure that week, until a good result lifted his mood and brought back memories of past successes.
slides.takeaway: Anxiety biases attention towards threat; mood biases memory towards matching experiences.

slides.heading: Classic theories in brief
slides.body:
Psychologists have long debated how body and mind combine in emotion. The **James-Lange** theory says we feel emotion **because** of bodily changes. The **Cannon-Bard** theory says body and feeling arise **together** from the brain. **Schachter and Singer's** two-factor theory says we **label** our arousal using cues from the situation.

Ekman's body patterns and LeDoux's fast amygdala route both feed into this debate.

slides.heading: How your lecturer will ask this
slides.body: Expect 'what neurochemicals are necessary for brain communication?' (transmitters, hormones, neuromodulators) and 'the role of the hypothalamus and septum'. Objectives test mood-congruent memory (Clark & Teasdale) and LeDoux's amygdala inputs. Note: the amygdala is a limbic structure in the temporal lobe, not part of the hypothalamus.
slides.sampleQuestion: Depressed participants recalled more unhappy memories at their most depressed time of day. This is known as: (a) state-dependent memory (b) mood-congruent memory (c) attunement (d) global empathy
slides.howToAnswer: Answer (b). Explain that memories matching current mood are more accessible (Clark & Teasdale, 1982).

points: Methods: lesions, stimulation and brain imaging.
Hypothalamus and septum process emotional and motivational information.
Amygdala: emotional computer with fast thalamic and slower cortical inputs.
Anxiety biases attention to threat; mood-congruent memory biases recall.

questions.stem: The brain structure often called the 'central emotional computer' is the:
questions.explanation: The amygdala integrates emotional information.

questions.stem: Which neurochemicals are carried in the blood to affect sensitive organs?
questions.explanation: Hormones travel in the blood to target organs.

questions.stem: Mood-congruent memory was demonstrated by:
questions.explanation: Clark and Teasdale (1982) showed recall matches current mood.

questions.stem: In the lesion method, psychologists study emotion by:
questions.explanation: Lesion studies look at what changes after damage to a brain area.

questions.stem: Many neuromodulators are peptides that:
options: Modulate the pain system and resemble opiates
questions.explanation: Peptide neuromodulators such as endorphins act on pain and resemble opiates.

questions.stem: Anxious individuals tend to show:
questions.explanation: Anxiety biases attention towards danger cues.

questions.stem: Researchers electrically stimulate a cat's brain region and observe sudden aggression. This method is:
questions.explanation: Stimulating an area and observing behaviour is the stimulation method.

questions.stem: A hiker leaps back from a curved stick before consciously recognising it. LeDoux would explain this through the:
options: Slow cortical route to the amygdala
Fast direct route from the thalamus to the amygdala
questions.explanation: The quick thalamus-amygdala route triggers fear before detailed recognition.

questions.stem: During a sad week, Emeka keeps remembering past disappointments. This illustrates:
questions.explanation: Recall biased towards mood-matching memories is mood-congruent memory.

questions.stem: All of the following are methods for studying brain and emotion EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Colour mixing relates to vision, not methods for studying emotion.

questions.stem: Which pair is correctly matched?
questions.explanation: Neuromodulators are often peptides affecting pain; transmitters act at synapses; hormones travel in blood.

questions.stem: The hypothalamus and septum together contribute to:
options: Processing emotional and motivational information and organising behaviour
questions.explanation: They process emotional and motivational signals to organise appropriate responses.

questions.stem: I. The amygdala receives input directly from the thalamus. II. Mood-congruent memory makes it easier to recall mood-matching memories. III. Depression improves recall of happy events. Which are correct?
questions.explanation: I and II are correct. Depression biases recall towards negative events.

questions.stem: Why might mood-congruent memory help keep depression going?
options: Low mood brings up sad memories, which deepen the low mood
questions.explanation: A self-reinforcing cycle forms between mood and recall.

questions.stem: A person's heart pounds after climbing stairs; meeting an attractive stranger at the top, they decide they are 'falling in love'. Which theory best explains this labelling?
questions.explanation: Two-factor theory says we label general arousal using situational cues, here wrongly as attraction.
